raw_evidence.label: TidyTuesday 2020-01-07: an emergency dataset release
raw_evidence.content: This dataset was released as part of TidyTuesday on 7 January 2020, in the middle of an active disaster. The official readme explicitly tells users to be cautious when plotting: the NSW Rural Fire Service major-incidents JSON was downloaded on 2020-01-06, and a NASA MODIS active-fire snapshot covers the seven days leading up to release. It was assembled less to drive a polished analysis than to let the data community see what was happening in real time. Unlike most TidyTuesday weeks that ship a single tidy CSV, this one bundles three very different sources: NASA satellite hotspots, NSW RFS incident polygons, and decades of Bureau of Meteorology weather records, with the South-East as the area most affected.

raw_evidence.label: MODIS FIRMS: how to read fire pixels honestly
raw_evidence.content: The fire data is from NASA's FIRMS / MODIS Collection 6 active-fire product. A row is not a fire — it is a 1 km satellite pixel that was thermally anomalous when MODIS passed overhead. NASA explicitly warns that FIRMS active fires should not be used to estimate burned area, because of nontrivial spatial and temporal sampling. MODIS detects roughly a quarter of fires recorded by ground agencies in the contiguous US; small under-canopy fires often go undetected because the canopy hides the heat signature. Because the MODIS bands do not perfectly distinguish heat sources, occasional pixels are gas flares, volcanic vents, or hot industrial roofs, not vegetation fire. Confidence is graded low / nominal / high, day or night. Daytime detections also pick up reflective surfaces, so the readme suggests night data for highest accuracy. Every chart we draw must respect this: we are mapping satellite detections, not ground truth.

raw_evidence.label: MODIS detected 34,248 fire pixels in eight days
raw_evidence.content: Across the seven-day window 2019-12-29 to 2020-01-05, MODIS satellites returned 34,248 thermal-anomaly pixels over mainland Australia. Detections were uneven by day: 6,936 pixels on December 30, dipping to 3,246-3,702 on December 29 / 31 / January 1, jumping to 4,394 and 4,273 on the next two days, then peaking at 7,384 on January 4 — the day NSW and Victoria coordinated mass evacuations from the South Coast — before dropping to just 867 on January 5 (the dataset cuts off mid-day). The hot pixels were not random noise: they tracked the operational tempo of the disaster.

print(daily.to_string(index=False))
print(f"total detections: {len(f):,}")

NASA MODIS hotspot file covers a 7-day window over Australia and New Zealand
weather data was sourced from BoM stations near Sydney, Perth, Brisbane, Canberra, Adelaide, Melbourne
the readme warns: 'PLEASE be cautious when plotting maps of ongoing fires'

raw_evidence.label: MODIS FIRMS: how to read fire pixels honestly
raw_evidence.content: The fire data is from NASA's FIRMS / MODIS Collection 6 active-fire product. A row is not a fire — it is a 1 km satellite pixel that was thermally anomalous when MODIS passed overhead. NASA explicitly warns that FIRMS active fires should not be used to estimate burned area, because of nontrivial spatial and temporal sampling. MODIS detects roughly a quarter of fires recorded by ground agencies in the contiguous US; small under-canopy fires often go undetected because the canopy hides the heat signature. Because the MODIS bands do not perfectly distinguish heat sources, occasional pixels are gas flares, volcanic vents, or hot industrial roofs, not vegetation fire. Confidence is graded low / nominal / high, day or night. Daytime detections also pick up reflective surfaces, so the readme suggests night data for highest accuracy. Every chart we draw must respect this: we are mapping satellite detections, not ground truth.

raw_evidence.label: Victoria contributed 59% of all detections
raw_evidence.content: Almost three out of every five MODIS detections in this window came from Victoria — 20,261 of 34,248 pixels (59.2%). New South Wales added 4,457 (13.0%), Western Australia 3,825 (11.2%), Queensland and inland scrub 4,138 combined, South Australia 1,227 (3.6%), and Tasmania just 340 (1.0%). The skew is striking given Victoria's modest physical size relative to Western Australia — and matches the press coverage of the East Gippsland fire complex (Victoria's south-eastern corner) being the single largest active front during this seven-day window.

raw_evidence.label: TidyTuesday 2020-01-07: an emergency dataset release
raw_evidence.content: This dataset was released as part of TidyTuesday on 7 January 2020, in the middle of an active disaster. The official readme explicitly tells users to be cautious when plotting: the NSW Rural Fire Service major-incidents JSON was downloaded on 2020-01-06, and a NASA MODIS active-fire snapshot covers the seven days leading up to release. It was assembled less to drive a polished analysis than to let the data community see what was happening in real time. Unlike most TidyTuesday weeks that ship a single tidy CSV, this one bundles three very different sources: NASA satellite hotspots, NSW RFS incident polygons, and decades of Bureau of Meteorology weather records, with the South-East as the area most affected.

raw_evidence.label: Map of high-confidence fire detections
raw_evidence.content: A scatter map of high-confidence MODIS detections (n=27,049) shows a continuous arc along the southeastern coast — from East Gippsland in Victoria up through the NSW South Coast and as far north as the Mid-North Coast and Queensland border. Tasmania and Western Australia have visible but isolated clusters; the WA cluster runs along the Nullarbor coast; the inland centroid is sparse. This is a satellite-eye view of Black Summer's first week.

print(f"sampled {len(sample)} of {len(hi):,} high-confidence detections; full hi total = {len(hi):,}")

raw_evidence.label: Map of high-confidence fire detections
raw_evidence.content: A scatter map of high-confidence MODIS detections (n=27,049) shows a continuous arc along the southeastern coast — from East Gippsland in Victoria up through the NSW South Coast and as far north as the Mid-North Coast and Queensland border. Tasmania and Western Australia have visible but isolated clusters; the WA cluster runs along the Nullarbor coast; the inland centroid is sparse. This is a satellite-eye view of Black Summer's first week.

raw_evidence.label: MODIS FIRMS: how to read fire pixels honestly
raw_evidence.content: The fire data is from NASA's FIRMS / MODIS Collection 6 active-fire product. A row is not a fire — it is a 1 km satellite pixel that was thermally anomalous when MODIS passed overhead. NASA explicitly warns that FIRMS active fires should not be used to estimate burned area, because of nontrivial spatial and temporal sampling. MODIS detects roughly a quarter of fires recorded by ground agencies in the contiguous US; small under-canopy fires often go undetected because the canopy hides the heat signature. Because the MODIS bands do not perfectly distinguish heat sources, occasional pixels are gas flares, volcanic vents, or hot industrial roofs, not vegetation fire. Confidence is graded low / nominal / high, day or night. Daytime detections also pick up reflective surfaces, so the readme suggests night data for highest accuracy. Every chart we draw must respect this: we are mapping satellite detections, not ground truth.

raw_evidence.label: 60% of Victorian detections were after dark
raw_evidence.content: The dangerous hallmark of Black Summer was night-time activity: in Victoria, 60.6% of MODIS detections were night pixels (12,270 of 20,261). New South Wales ran 53.5% night detections. Most other regions sat closer to a normal day-skewed pattern (WA 26.6%, SA 14.3%). Night fire is operationally menacing — humidity recovery stops, crews fatigue, and the firefronts continue to advance — and the night-share data in this seven-day window confirms why Victorian and NSW agencies were unable to gain ground at night.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_13: night-fire share by region (night burns are more dangerous) ---
print("=== ana_13 ===")
night = f.groupby(["region", "daynight"]).size().unstack(fill_value=0)
night["total"] = night.sum(axis=1)
night["night_pct"] = (night["N"] / night["total"] * 100).round(1)
night = night.sort_values("total", ascending=False)
print(night.to_string())
raw_evidence.output: VIC 60.6% night; NSW 53.5%; QLD 41.3%; TAS 42.1%; WA 26.6%; SA 14.3%; QLD/NT/SA inland 27.8%

raw_evidence.label: FRP distribution — most pixels modest, top 1% above 1.6 GW
raw_evidence.content: Fire Radiative Power on these pixels has a long, heavy right tail: the median pixel released 38.7 megawatts, the mean 125.3 MW (skewed by a few giants), the 90th percentile 266.8 MW, the 99th percentile 1,657 MW, and the maximum a single pixel at 7,109 MW. By bucket, 31.3% of pixels released under 25 MW, 42.6% sat in the 25-100 MW band, 20.5% reached 100-500 MW, and 5.6% — almost 1,800 pixels — exceeded 500 MW. The long tail is what produced the pyrocumulonimbus events Australian fire managers reported in this period.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_11: fire radiative power (FRP) distribution ---
print("=== ana_11 ===")
print(f"FRP MW: median={f['frp'].median():.1f}, mean={f['frp'].mean():.1f}, p90={f['frp'].quantile(0.9):.1f}, p99={f['frp'].quantile(0.99):.1f}, max={f['frp'].max():.1f}")
# count by bucket
fp = pd.cut(f["frp"], bins=[0, 25, 100, 500, 10000], labels=["<25 MW", "25-100", "100-500", "500+"])
fpv = fp.value_counts().reindex(["<25 MW", "25-100", "100-500", "500+"]).reset_index()
fpv.columns = ["frp_class", "count"]
fpv["pct"] = (fpv["count"] / fpv["count"].sum() * 100).round(1)
print(fpv.to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.content: The fire data is from NASA's FIRMS / MODIS Collection 6 active-fire product. A row is not a fire — it is a 1 km satellite pixel that was thermally anomalous when MODIS passed overhead. Confidence is graded low / nominal / high, day or night. Daytime detections also pick up reflective surfaces, so the readme suggests night data for highest accuracy. sentences.context: The driest year, almost everywhere
sentences.summary: det_03: 2019: hottest and driest year on record. Source: Annual climate statement 2019 — Bureau of Meteorology (https://www.bom.gov.au/climate/current/annual/aus/2019/) Facts: annual mean temperature 1.52 °C above 1961-1990 average; maximum temperature anomaly +2.09 °C — first time over 2 °C

raw_evidence.label: 2019: hottest and driest year on record
raw_evidence.content: 2019 was simultaneously Australia's hottest and driest year on record — the first time since overlapping records began that both extremes occurred in the same calendar year. Annual mean temperature was 1.52 °C above the 1961-1990 average, the previous record (1.33 °C, 2013) shattered. Maximum temperatures ran +2.09 °C above the long-term average — the first time the country crossed a +2 °C anomaly. Area-averaged rainfall was just 277.6 mm against a long-term average of 465.2 mm. For the first time, every single month of the year was below the national rainfall average. This is the climatological pre-condition the fire data sits on top of.

raw_evidence.label: Canberra's driest year on record was 2019
raw_evidence.content: Ranking 2019 against the full historical record at each station produces an even harsher reading. In Canberra, 2019 (358.6 mm) was the single driest year in the available 11-year station record. Brisbane's 2019 was the 5th-driest of 42 years, Perth's 5th of 52, Melbourne's 7th of 49, and Sydney's 19th of 161 — but every one of these falls in the bottom 12-15% of years on record. Sydney's all-time driest year remains 1888 at 583 mm, but that record was set by a 19th-century drought; 2019 ranks among the worst years of the modern era at every station the dataset can score.

print("=== ana_05 ===")

    if (sub["year"] == 2019).any():
        rank_2019 = int(sub.index[sub["year"] == 2019][0]) + 1
        total_yrs = len(sub)
        driest = sub.iloc[0]
        print(f"{c}: 2019 rank = {rank_2019} of {total_yrs} ({rank_2019/total_yrs*100:.1f} pctl); driest year overall = {int(driest['year'])} at {driest['annual_mm']:.0f} mm")

raw_evidence.label: Spring 2019 collapse — November and December were nearly bone dry
raw_evidence.content: The shape of the 2019 deficit was not uniform across months: it was a late-spring/early-summer collapse exactly when Australia's fire fuel finishes drying out. Canberra received 1.2 mm in December against an 84.7 mm climatology (-83.5 mm); Sydney 1.6 mm against 77.6 mm (-76.0 mm); Melbourne 4.4 mm against 62.3 mm (-57.9 mm); Brisbane 9.6 mm in November against 135.3 mm (-125.7 mm); Perth 2.6 mm in December against 10.0 mm. By contrast, March and June 2019 were near-average or wetter than usual at several stations — the 2019 drought was concentrated in the months that mattered most for fire weather.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_06 ===")
rain["month_num"] = pd.to_numeric(rain["month"], errors="coerce")
clim = rain[rain["year"] < 2019].groupby(["city_name", "month_num"])["rainfall"].sum().reset_index()
clim_avg = clim.groupby(["city_name", "month_num"])["rainfall"].mean().reset_index()
# Better: use sum per (city, year, month) then average across years
mset = rain.groupby(["city_name", "year", "month_num"])["rainfall"].sum().reset_index()
clim_avg = mset[mset["year"] < 2019].groupby(["city_name", "month_num"])["rainfall"].mean().reset_index()
clim_avg.columns = ["city_name", "month_num", "avg_mm"]
y2019m = mset[mset["year"] == 2019].rename(columns={"rainfall": "y2019_mm"})
m = clim_avg.merge(y2019m[["city_name", "month_num", "y2019_mm"]], on=["city_name", "month_num"], how="left")
m["delta_mm"] = (m["y2019_mm"] - m["avg_mm"]).round(1)
print(m.to_string(index=False))
raw_evidence.output: Canberra Dec -83.5 mm; Sydney Dec -76.0 mm; Melbourne Dec -57.9 mm; Brisbane Nov -125.7 mm

raw_evidence.label: Climate attribution: a 30%+ rise in fire weather risk
raw_evidence.content: The World Weather Attribution rapid-attribution study found that anthropogenic climate change has raised the Fire Weather Index in the affected region by at least 30 %, driven mostly by extreme heat. Heat extremes of the 2019-20 magnitude have become at least twice as likely under long-term warming. The drought that primed the fuel had a more complex story — a coincidence of two consecutive positive Indian Ocean Dipole events with a Central Pacific El Niño, which climate change is making more frequent. The conclusion: the fire weather of Black Summer is not a one-off; it is what an early-21st-century Australian summer can now look like.

raw_evidence.content: Pooling the five long-record cities, 2019 sits at 26.40 C — the highest annual mean daily maximum in the entire 1910-2019 window and roughly 3 C above the surrounding decade. The shape of the curve is gradual warming through the 20th century followed by a step-function jump in 2019, exactly the climatological pre-condition the Bureau of Meteorology described in its 2019 Annual Climate Statement.

raw_evidence.label: 2019: hottest and driest year on record
raw_evidence.content: 2019 was simultaneously Australia's hottest and driest year on record — the first time since overlapping records began that both extremes occurred in the same calendar year. Annual mean temperature was 1.52 °C above the 1961-1990 average, the previous record (1.33 °C, 2013) shattered. Maximum temperatures ran +2.09 °C above the long-term average — the first time the country crossed a +2 °C anomaly. Area-averaged rainfall was just 277.6 mm against a long-term average of 465.2 mm. For the first time, every single month of the year was below the national rainfall average. This is the climatological pre-condition the fire data sits on top of.

raw_evidence.label: Climate attribution: a 30%+ rise in fire weather risk
raw_evidence.content: The World Weather Attribution rapid-attribution study found that anthropogenic climate change has raised the Fire Weather Index in the affected region by at least 30 %, driven mostly by extreme heat. Heat extremes of the 2019-20 magnitude have become at least twice as likely under long-term warming. The drought that primed the fuel had a more complex story — a coincidence of two consecutive positive Indian Ocean Dipole events with a Central Pacific El Niño, which climate change is making more frequent. The conclusion: the fire weather of Black Summer is not a one-off; it is what an early-21st-century Australian summer can now look like.

raw_evidence.label: Capital cities have warmed 1.2-2.4 C since 1910-1940
raw_evidence.content: Comparing the 2010-2019 decade to the 1910-1940 baseline, every Australian capital with continuous records has warmed substantially. Canberra leads at +2.39 C (19.14 -> 21.53 C mean daily maximum), followed by Perth at +2.10 C (23.73 -> 25.82 C), Melbourne at +1.62 C, and Sydney at +1.17 C. Brisbane lacks pre-1949 data so cannot be compared on the same baseline; its 2010-2019 mean is 25.64 C. These are city-station maxima, not national averages, but the direction is unambiguous: every comparable city is hotter than it was a century ago by between one and almost two and a half degrees.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_01 ===")
tmax = temp[temp["temp_type"] == "max"].copy()
yearly = tmax.groupby(["city_name", "year"])["temperature"].mean().reset_index()

# Baseline 1910-1940, recent 2010-2019
base = yearly[(yearly["year"] >= 1910) & (yearly["year"] <= 1940)].groupby("city_name")["temperature"].mean()
recent = yearly[(yearly["year"] >= 2010) & (yearly["year"] <= 2019)].groupby("city_name")["temperature"].mean()
delta = (recent - base).round(2)
out = pd.DataFrame({"baseline_1910_1940_C": base.round(2), "recent_2010_2019_C": recent.round(2), "delta_C": delta})
out = out.sort_values("delta_C", ascending=False)
print(out.to_string())
raw_evidence.output: Canberra +2.39 C; Perth +2.10 C; Melbourne +1.62 C; Sydney +1.17 C; Brisbane n/a (no baseline)

raw_evidence.editorial_notes: 26.4 C is the load-bearing 2019 anomaly. Decadal city deltas (Canberra +2.39, Perth +2.10) anchor the long-run warming.

raw_evidence.label: 2019: hottest and driest year on record
raw_evidence.content: 2019 was simultaneously Australia's hottest and driest year on record — the first time since overlapping records began that both extremes occurred in the same calendar year. Annual mean temperature was 1.52 °C above the 1961-1990 average, the previous record (1.33 °C, 2013) shattered. Maximum temperatures ran +2.09 °C above the long-term average — the first time the country crossed a +2 °C anomaly. Area-averaged rainfall was just 277.6 mm against a long-term average of 465.2 mm. For the first time, every single month of the year was below the national rainfall average. This is the climatological pre-condition the fire data sits on top of.

raw_evidence.label: Per-city warming series for small multiples
raw_evidence.content: When the mean-daily-maximum series is broken out by city, every city shows a long-run warming signal but the slopes differ. Canberra rises from a first-decade mean of 18.61 C to a final-decade mean of 21.53 C (delta +2.92 C). Perth runs +2.41 C, Melbourne +1.57 C, Brisbane +0.90 C, Sydney +0.83 C. The 2019 value in every city visibly breaks above the prior decade's range, consistent with the national 2019 anomaly observed in ana_02.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_03 ===")
city_yearly = (
    tmax.groupby(["city_name", "year"])["temperature"].mean().reset_index().rename(columns={"temperature": "mean_max_C"})
)
city_yearly = city_yearly[(city_yearly["year"] >= 1910) & (city_yearly["year"] <= 2019)]
# Show the per-city deltas one more time with clean numbers.
for c in CITIES:
    sub = city_yearly[city_yearly["city_name"] == c].sort_values("year")
    if len(sub) > 0:
        first = sub.head(10)["mean_max_C"].mean()
        last = sub.tail(10)["mean_max_C"].mean()
        print(f"{c}: first 10y = {first:.2f}, last 10y = {last:.2f}, delta = {last - first:+.2f} C")

city_yearly.to_csv(f"{DATA.replace('data_preprint', 'data_preprint')}/_temp_city_yearly.csv", index=False)
raw_evidence.output: Brisbane +0.90 C; Canberra +2.92 C; Melbourne +1.57 C; Perth +2.41 C; Sydney +0.83 C (first 10y vs last 10y)

raw_evidence.label: 2019: hottest and driest year on record
raw_evidence.content: 2019 was simultaneously Australia's hottest and driest year on record — the first time since overlapping records began that both extremes occurred in the same calendar year. Annual mean temperature was 1.52 °C above the 1961-1990 average, the previous record (1.33 °C, 2013) shattered. Maximum temperatures ran +2.09 °C above the long-term average — the first time the country crossed a +2 °C anomaly. Area-averaged rainfall was just 277.6 mm against a long-term average of 465.2 mm. For the first time, every single month of the year was below the national rainfall average. This is the climatological pre-condition the fire data sits on top of.

raw_evidence.label: Climate attribution: a 30%+ rise in fire weather risk
raw_evidence.content: The World Weather Attribution rapid-attribution study found that anthropogenic climate change has raised the Fire Weather Index in the affected region by at least 30 %, driven mostly by extreme heat. Heat extremes of the 2019-20 magnitude have become at least twice as likely under long-term warming. The drought that primed the fuel had a more complex story — a coincidence of two consecutive positive Indian Ocean Dipole events with a Central Pacific El Niño, which climate change is making more frequent. The conclusion: the fire weather of Black Summer is not a one-off; it is what an early-21st-century Australian summer can now look like.

raw_evidence.label: Six cities, one continent: the BoM weather panel
raw_evidence.content: The Bureau of Meteorology data in this dataset is not a national average — it is six (sometimes seven) hand-picked stations near the largest cities: Perth (Subiaco WWTP, 009151), Adelaide (North Adelaide, 023011), Brisbane (Greenslopes Hospital, 040383, plus Brisbane city 040913), Sydney (Observatory Hill, 066062), Canberra (Airport, 070351) and Melbourne (Botanical Gardens, 086232). Observatory Hill, in particular, has rainfall back to 1858 and temperature back to 1859 — among the longest continuous urban records in the Southern Hemisphere. Most of the climate signal in this analysis is therefore the South-East corner of Australia, exactly the region the readme flags as 'most affected'.

raw_evidence.label: Per-city warming series for small multiples
raw_evidence.content: When the mean-daily-maximum series is broken out by city, every city shows a long-run warming signal but the slopes differ. Canberra rises from a first-decade mean of 18.61 C to a final-decade mean of 21.53 C (delta +2.92 C). Perth runs +2.41 C, Melbourne +1.57 C, Brisbane +0.90 C, Sydney +0.83 C. The 2019 value in every city visibly breaks above the prior decade's range, consistent with the national 2019 anomaly observed in ana_02.

raw_evidence.label: Black Summer: the season behind the data
raw_evidence.content: The 2019-20 Australian bushfire season — known as the Black Summer — burned roughly 24 million hectares of land, an area larger than the United Kingdom. Thirty-three people died directly in the fires; an additional ~417 deaths were attributed to bushfire smoke. Around 3,094 homes were destroyed. The wildlife toll, the most cited number from this event, is approximately 3 billion native vertebrates killed or displaced (mostly reptiles), with up to 60,000 koalas affected and an estimated 40,000 koalas perishing on Kangaroo Island alone. The fire pixels in the MODIS file are this season — sampled in its first week.

Pairing this with MODIS lets a story confirm: when satellites saw a hotspot in the South East coast, RFS was almost certainly running an active incident on the ground. The RFS feed is the link between abstract pixels and the people and equipment fighting them.

raw_evidence.label: Hectares vs satellite pixels: the scale gap
raw_evidence.content: The two fire products in this dataset measure different things. The seven-day MODIS file is a snapshot — bright pixels in a one-week window. The full Black Summer burned-area total of ~24 million hectares is a season-long ground accounting from agencies. A 1 km MODIS pixel covers ~100 hectares; if we naively multiplied the ~34,000 detection rows by 100 ha we would massively overcount, because the same fire is re-detected on every overpass and many pixels overlap. The benchmark to use is the official seasonal total, not the satellite count. The dataset is a slice of an event whose full scale is documented elsewhere.

raw_evidence.label: 143 NSW major incidents on January 6 — 31 still out of control
raw_evidence.content: On the morning of January 6, 2020 — the day this dataset was downloaded — the NSW Rural Fire Service reported 143 declared major incidents. Of those, 82 were under control, 30 being controlled, and 31 still out of control. By type, 126 were bush fires, 9 grass fires, and a long tail of medical, transport, and storm-related incidents that show the RFS feed captured every active call, not only fires. All but 15 carried an Advice alert level (the lowest of three levels), reflecting the snapshot mid-week — the major Watch & Act / Emergency Warning escalations that defined the New Year's Eve days had subsided by the 6th.

alert_counts = Counter()
type_counts = Counter()
size_total_ha = 0.0
sizes = []
for f in feats:
    p = f.get("properties", {})
    parsed = parse_props(p)
    status_counts[parsed.get("STATUS", "Unknown")] += 1
    alert_counts[parsed.get("ALERT LEVEL", "Unknown")] += 1
    type_counts[parsed.get("TYPE", "Unknown")] += 1
    sz = parsed.get("SIZE", "0 ha")
    m = re.match(r"([\d,]+(?:\.\d+)?)\s*ha", sz)
    if m:
        v = float(m.group(1).replace(",", ""))
        sizes.append(v)
        size_total_ha += v

print("status:")
for k, v in status_counts.most_common():

    print(f"  {k}: {v}")
print("type:")

    print(f"  {k}: {v}")

raw_evidence.label: 143 NSW major incidents on January 6 — 31 still out of control
raw_evidence.content: On the morning of January 6, 2020 — the day this dataset was downloaded — the NSW Rural Fire Service reported 143 declared major incidents. raw_evidence.label: Gospers Mountain alone burned 511,661 hectares
raw_evidence.content: The 15 largest NSW incidents in this snapshot read like a roll call of Black Summer's most devastating fires. Gospers Mountain, in Wollemi National Park, sat at 511,661 hectares — the largest single forest fire ever from a single ignition in Australian history (a lightning strike on October 26, 2019). Dunns Road, second on the list, was 313,536 ha and still officially out of control. Currowan, Green Wattle Creek, Carrai Creek, Badja Forest Road, Green Valley, and Little L Complex all individually exceeded 150,000 hectares. Across all 99 incidents with declared sizes, total declared area was 4.0 million hectares of NSW alone — out of the season's eventual ~24 million hectare national total.

raw_evidence.label: Black Summer: the season behind the data
raw_evidence.content: The 2019-20 Australian bushfire season — known as the Black Summer — burned roughly 24 million hectares of land, an area larger than the United Kingdom. Thirty-three people died directly in the fires; an additional ~417 deaths were attributed to bushfire smoke. Around 3,094 homes were destroyed. The wildlife toll, the most cited number from this event, is approximately 3 billion native vertebrates killed or displaced (mostly reptiles), with up to 60,000 koalas affected and an estimated 40,000 koalas perishing on Kangaroo Island alone. raw_evidence.label: Hectares vs satellite pixels: the scale gap
raw_evidence.content: The two fire products in this dataset measure different things. The seven-day MODIS file is a snapshot — bright pixels in a one-week window. The full Black Summer burned-area total of ~24 million hectares is a season-long ground accounting from agencies. A 1 km MODIS pixel covers ~100 hectares; if we naively multiplied the ~34,000 detection rows by 100 ha we would massively overcount, because the same fire is re-detected on every overpass and many pixels overlap. The benchmark to use is the official seasonal total, not the satellite count. The dataset is a slice of an event whose full scale is documented elsewhere.

raw_evidence.label: Gospers Mountain alone burned 511,661 hectares
raw_evidence.content: The 15 largest NSW incidents in this snapshot read like a roll call of Black Summer's most devastating fires. Gospers Mountain, in Wollemi National Park, sat at 511,661 hectares — the largest single forest fire ever from a single ignition in Australian history (a lightning strike on October 26, 2019). Dunns Road, second on the list, was 313,536 ha and still officially out of control. Currowan, Green Wattle Creek, Carrai Creek, Badja Forest Road, Green Valley, and Little L Complex all individually exceeded 150,000 hectares. Across all 99 incidents with declared sizes, total declared area was 4.0 million hectares of NSW alone — out of the season's eventual ~24 million hectare national total.

raw_evidence.label: Black Summer: the season behind the data
raw_evidence.content: The 2019-20 Australian bushfire season — known as the Black Summer — burned roughly 24 million hectares of land, an area larger than the United Kingdom. Thirty-three people died directly in the fires; an additional ~417 deaths were attributed to bushfire smoke. Around 3,094 homes were destroyed. The wildlife toll, the most cited number from this event, is approximately 3 billion native vertebrates killed or displaced (mostly reptiles), with up to 60,000 koalas affected and an estimated 40,000 koalas perishing on Kangaroo Island alone. The fire pixels in the MODIS file are this season — sampled in its first week.

The RFS feed is the link between abstract pixels and the people and equipment fighting them.

raw_evidence.label: MODIS FIRMS: how to read fire pixels honestly
raw_evidence.content: The fire data is from NASA's FIRMS / MODIS Collection 6 active-fire product. A row is not a fire — it is a 1 km satellite pixel that was thermally anomalous when MODIS passed overhead. NASA explicitly warns that FIRMS active fires should not be used to estimate burned area, because of nontrivial spatial and temporal sampling. MODIS detects roughly a quarter of fires recorded by ground agencies in the contiguous US; small under-canopy fires often go undetected because the canopy hides the heat signature. Because the MODIS bands do not perfectly distinguish heat sources, occasional pixels are gas flares, volcanic vents, or hot industrial roofs, not vegetation fire. Confidence is graded low / nominal / high, day or night. Daytime detections also pick up reflective surfaces, so the readme suggests night data for highest accuracy. Every chart we draw must respect this: we are mapping satellite detections, not ground truth.

raw_evidence.label: MODIS FIRMS: how to read fire pixels honestly
raw_evidence.content: The fire data is from NASA's FIRMS / MODIS Collection 6 active-fire product. A row is not a fire — it is a 1 km satellite pixel that was thermally anomalous when MODIS passed overhead. NASA explicitly warns that FIRMS active fires should not be used to estimate burned area, because of nontrivial spatial and temporal sampling. MODIS detects roughly a quarter of fires recorded by ground agencies in the contiguous US; small under-canopy fires often go undetected because the canopy hides the heat signature. Because the MODIS bands do not perfectly distinguish heat sources, occasional pixels are gas flares, volcanic vents, or hot industrial roofs, not vegetation fire. Confidence is graded low / nominal / high, day or night. Daytime detections also pick up reflective surfaces, so the readme suggests night data for highest accuracy. Every chart we draw must respect this: we are mapping satellite detections, not ground truth.

raw_evidence.label: Hectares vs satellite pixels: the scale gap
raw_evidence.content: The two fire products in this dataset measure different things. The seven-day MODIS file is a snapshot — bright pixels in a one-week window. The full Black Summer burned-area total of ~24 million hectares is a season-long ground accounting from agencies. A 1 km MODIS pixel covers ~100 hectares; if we naively multiplied the ~34,000 detection rows by 100 ha we would massively overcount, because the same fire is re-detected on every overpass and many pixels overlap. The benchmark to use is the official seasonal total, not the satellite count. The dataset is a slice of an event whose full scale is documented elsewhere.

raw_evidence.label: TidyTuesday 2020-01-07: an emergency dataset release
raw_evidence.content: This dataset was released as part of TidyTuesday on 7 January 2020, in the middle of an active disaster. The official readme explicitly tells users to be cautious when plotting: the NSW Rural Fire Service major-incidents JSON was downloaded on 2020-01-06, and a NASA MODIS active-fire snapshot covers the seven days leading up to release. It was assembled less to drive a polished analysis than to let the data community see what was happening in real time. Unlike most TidyTuesday weeks that ship a single tidy CSV, this one bundles three very different sources: NASA satellite hotspots, NSW RFS incident polygons, and decades of Bureau of Meteorology weather records, with the South-East as the area most affected.
